description: Two overlapping glass panels over colored shapes: the second one's backdrop already contains the first one's blurred, tinted result, and the first keeps its own blur where the second does not cover it.

florui.css: .scene { position: relative; width: 220px; height: 150px; background-color: #1b1b2f; overflow: hidden; } .s1 { position: absolute; left: 10px; top: 14px; width: 100px; height: 100px; background-color: #ff5a5f; border-radius: 50px; } .s2 { position: absolute; left: 100px; top: 40px; width: 100px; height: 80px; background-color: #2ec4b6; } .s3 { position: absolute; left: 30px; top: 100px; width: 120px; height: 36px; background-color: #ffd166; } .a { position: absolute; left: 24px; top: 24px; width: 110px; height: 70px; border-radius: 18px; background-color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.16); backdrop-filter: blur(6px) saturate(1.4); } .b { position: absolute; left: 84px; top: 56px; width: 110px; height: 70px; border-radius: 18px; background-color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.16); backdrop-filter: blur(6px) saturate(1.4); }

classification.reason: Chromium and this engine build a Gaussian blur differently (kernel shape and rounding), so a pixel in the blurred area differs by a few levels of 255 and a pixel at a steep colour edge by more. Measured against desktop Chrome: 0.25% differ by more than 8 levels (20% by any amount, mean error 0.4, max 28). channel_tolerance 8 stops the harmless rounding from counting; the percentage left is the steep edges. With the backdrop blur read past the panel edge as transparent instead of mirrored (the defect this fixture found), about 30% of the pixels differed by more than that.
